title: 2 Kings 14:23–29
context: Jeroboam son of Joash, often called Jeroboam II, reigns forty-one years in Samaria and continues in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Yet he restores Israel’s borders according to the word of the LORD through Jonah son of Amittai, because the LORD saw Israel’s bitter affliction and chose to save them through Jeroboam. The passage holds together an evil king and a merciful God. Both traditions read it as shared ground about God’s compassion and faithfulness to his word, and Judges 9:23 and Judges 10:16 already treat the related questions.

verses.text: In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel began to reign in Samaria for forty-one years.
verses.arminianNotes:
In Amaziah’s fifteenth year, Jeroboam son of Joash begins a forty-one-year reign over Israel in Samaria. His reign is long.

Arminian readers see Jeroboam given a long span of time and opportunity before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
This king is often called Jeroboam II. Some propose that the forty-one years include a coregency with his father, though this remains a reconstruction.

Reformed readers see God appointing the length of reigns. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hedge the chronology.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight. He didn’t depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam does evil and does not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. The verdict matches his predecessors’.

Arminian readers see a king who freely continues the idolatry he inherited despite God’s mercies.
verses.reformedNotes:
The two Jeroboams are linked by name and by sin. The northern pattern remains unbroken.

Reformed readers see the persistence of entrenched idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and they note that God’s mercy in the following verses comes despite this verdict, not because of it.

verses.text: He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah, according to the LORD, the God of Israel’s word, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath Hepher.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam restores Israel’s border from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah, according to the LORD’s word through Jonah son of Amittai from Gath Hepher. Prophecy is fulfilled.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious word coming true.
verses.reformedNotes:
This Jonah is generally identified with the prophet of the book of Jonah (Jonah 1:1), whose oracle here is not otherwise recorded.

Reformed readers see God keeping his spoken word. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: For the LORD saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter for all, slave and free; and there was no helper for Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sees Israel’s bitter affliction, slave and free alike, and that there is no helper for Israel. God notices their suffering.

Arminian readers see God’s compassion freely moved by his people’s distress (compare the box at Judges 10:16).
verses.reformedNotes:
The language recalls 13:4, where the LORD saw Israel’s oppression. No human help is available.

Reformed readers see God’s mercy as the only source of rescue. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s pity toward the helpless.

verses.text: The LORD didn’t say that he would blot out the name of Israel from under the sky; but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD has not said he will blot out Israel’s name, and he saves them by the hand of Jeroboam. God uses an evil king to deliver.

Arminian readers see mercy freely extended to an undeserving people, still inviting repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The word ‘saved’ is applied to deliverance through a king the narrator has just judged as evil (v. 24).

Reformed readers see God using an imperfect instrument for his purposes; Judges 9:23 treats how God works through such agents. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, and all that he did, and his might, how he fought, and how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath, which had belonged to Judah, for Israel, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Jeroboam’s acts, his might, and how he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Israel are referred to Israel’s chronicles. His reign was militarily significant.

Arminian readers see real success granted to Israel in this period.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase about Damascus and Hamath ‘which had belonged to Judah’ is difficult; interpreters often connect it with the extent of David’s and Solomon’s rule, but certainty is lacking.

Reformed readers see God’s kindness to Israel. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Jeroboam slept with his fathers, even with the kings of Israel; and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeroboam dies and rests with the kings of Israel, and his son Zechariah reigns in his place. The dynasty continues another generation.

Arminian readers see the close of a prosperous but unfaithful reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zechariah will be the fourth generation of Jehu’s sons on the throne, fulfilling the promise of 2 Kings 10:30 (see 2 Kings 15:12).

Reformed readers see God keeping his word to Jehu precisely. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness.
